question: Does chronic sleep restriction impair memory consolidation?

starFinding.text: Yes — chronic sleep restriction impairs memory consolidation, with the hippocampus emerging as selectively vulnerable across all eight studies.
starFinding.sourceQuote: Sleep deprivation is detrimental to hippocampus-dependent memory.

top3.text: Sleep deprivation during the first 5 hours after training impairs consolidation of contextual fear conditioning, establishing a critical early consolidation window.
top3.sourceQuote: Graves et al. demonstrated that sleep deprivation from 0-5 hours after training impaired memory consolidation for contextual fear conditioning, whereas sleep deprivation from 5-10 hours post-training had no effect [Graves et al., 2003].

top3.text: The impairment is molecularly reversible: restoring hippocampal mTORC1 signaling prevented the memory deficits caused by sleep loss, demonstrating a causal pathway.
top3.sourceQuote: Increasing 4EBP2 protein levels restored hippocampal mTORC1 signaling in sleep-deprived mice and prevented memory deficits associated with sleep loss [Havekes & Abel, 2017], demonstrating causal involvement of this pathway.

top3.text: Sleep restriction impaired hippocampus-dependent learning and abolished learning-induced neurogenesis, while selectively sparing (even improving) non-hippocampal tasks.
top3.sourceQuote: Hairston et al. demonstrated that sleep restriction not only impaired hippocampus-dependent learning but also abolished learning-induced neurogenesis [Hairston et al., 2005].

doNotPromote: Diekelmann & Born (2010) — 'Not mentioned' per Elicit; a background claim that sleep optimizes consolidation of newly acquired information, which does not address the impact of chronic sleep restriction and must not be ranked #1.
Graves et al. (2003) null result — sleep deprivation from 5-10 hours after training had no effect; this off-window negative finding must not be promoted as the headline answer.
